documentation.range:
Following the revision of the Bufo viridis complex by Stöck et al. (2006) and the further work of Dufresnes et al. (2019), subpopulations of Green Toads now allocated to this species are distributed through much of Europe (excluding much of Fenno-Skandia, the British Isles, almost the entirety of Italy, the Iberian Peninsula and almost all of Europe west of the Rhine River) eastwards to Kazakhstan. It exhibits a contact zone with Bufotes sitibundus that roughly corresponds to the Volga River and appears to represent its natural eastern range limit; an isolated subpopulation along the Ob River in Siberia is likely to represent a human introduction (Dufresnes et al. 2019). 

Following genetic analysis, Bufotes variabilis has also been placed in synonymy with this species (Dufresnes et al. 2019) such that this species' range now includes subpopulations from the Eastern Mediterranean countries, and much of Central and Middle Asia (as Bufotes variabilis in Stöck et al. 2006). It is possible that subpopulations from the southern tip of Sweden, Denmark and northern Germany that were provisionally identified as Bufotes (Bufo) variabilis by Stöck et al. (2006) belong to this species. The species of Green Toad on the island of Malta is unclear, and is retained here in Bufotes viridis pending further research. 

Subpopulations from North Africa are now assigned to Bufotes boulengeri. Subpopulations of Green Toads from the Balearic Islands (Spain), Corsica (France), Sardinia (Italy) and much of mainland Italy are now recognized as Bufotes balearicus. Green Toad subpopulations from Sicily, Italy, now mostly comprise the endemic Bufotes siculus, with some subpopulations of Bufotes balearicus in the northeast of this island. The status of Green Toads in Israel, Jordan, Sinai (Egypt) and the isolated, relict subpopulation in the southern Hadramaut in southwestern Saudi Arabia (where recent records are restricted to three localities in the Sodah Mountains; Al-Qahatani and Al-Johany 2018) is currently unclear, and it is possible that these subpopulations should be included in this species or Bufotes boulengeri pending further review. Dufresnes et al. (2019) refer to these latter subpopulations as "Bufotes cf. sitibundus" and tentatively treat them as a subspecies of this taxon pending further review.
documentation.population: This species is still considered a relatively abundant to common species over large parts of its range, although subpopulations formally recognized as Bufotes viridis are rare or declining on the fringes of its range in Europe (e.g. Denmark and Sweden). It is extinct in Switzerland despite re-introduction efforts. Declines have been observed in Czechia (A. Krása pers. comm. September 2019), have occurred in Romania due to urbanisation (D. Cogălniceanu pers. comm. September 2019), and it is not as common as it was 20 years ago in Bucharest, Hungary (E. Mizsei pers. comm. September 2019). It is suspected to be decreasing in Bulgaria (Y. Kornilev, G. Popgeorgiev and B. Naumov pers. comm. October 2019). However, the species is fine in Italy (F. Ficetola and R. Manenti pers. comm. September 2019).
documentation.habitats: This species lives in a wide range of forests, forest steppe, scrubland, grassland and alpine habitats. Animals may be present in modified areas including urban centres (e.g., Bucharest), city parks and gardens - and often benefit from disturbed habitats. Spawning and larval development occur in a diverse range of temporary and permanent waterbodies including swamps, ponds, lakes, pools in streams and rivers, reservoirs, ditches and puddles.
documentation.threats: The main threat over much of its range, especially in the north, appears to be the loss of breeding habitats through wetland drainage, desiccation and aquatic pollution (industrial and agricultural). Subpopulations might be locally declining due to mortality on roads. In Czechia, an increase in fish farms and exotic fish introductions has been detrimental to the species (A. Krása pers. comm. September 2019) and, while the species is fairly adaptable, urbansiation has been a problem for its Romanian subpopulation (D. Cogălniceanu pers. comm. September 2019). Collection for the national and international pet trade may be an additional threat.
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
The species is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention and is listed on Annex IV of the EU Natural Habitats Directive. It is protected by national legislation in many countries; it is recorded on many national and sub-national Red Data books and lists and is present in many protected areas. In parts of this species' range, mitigation measures to reduce road kill have been established. 

Conservation Needed
Al Qahtani and Al-Johany (2018) recommend urgent protection for remaining wetlands in Saudi Arabia to ensure the persistence of amphibians in this country.

Research Needed
Further taxonomic work is needed to clarify the identity of some subpopulations. More research is needed into the species' distribution, population trends and threats. Monitoring of subpopulations believed to be in decline is also necessary.
documentation.use_trade: It may be collected for the national and international pet trade.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a range of habitats, and presumed large population.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Further revision of taxonomy of the Bufotes viridis complex with the use of genetic and biochemical data is needed. There was disagreement over the use of the generic name Pseudepidalea in place of Bufo and now most species have been moved to Bufotes because of non-monophyly of both Bufo and Pseudepidalea.

After Dufresnes et al. (2019) revised the taxonomy of the B. viridis complex, synonymizing B. balearicus and Bufo variabilis within it and clarified range limits between this species and the former synonym B. sitibundus, which they elevated to specific status, encompassing most of the species' former range, Frost ("Amphibian Species of the World") again synonymized B. sitibundus with B. viridis. Bufo perrini was also elevated from sub-species to species level by Dufresnes et al. (2019), but is not recognised by Frost as a separate taxonomic entity.
